Nicholas Barbon (1640–1698) is little appreciated by most historians of economic thought. He is sporadically mentioned in a few writings—probably the most well-known being the favorable reference to him made by John Maynard Keynes (1883–1946) in The General Theory of Employment, Interest, and Money (Keynes 1936, p. 359). The fullest treatment of Barbon's economic ideas is contained in The Origin of Scientific Economics: English Economic Thought 1660–1776 by William Louis Letwin (Letwin 1963, pp. 48–75). Nicholas Barbon

Nicholas Barbon (born c. 1640, London—died 1698) was an English economist, widely considered the founder of fire insurance.
Barbon was probably the son of the sectarian preacher Praise-God Barbon. He studied medicine at the University of Leiden, received his M.D. at Utrecht in 1661, and became an honorary fellow of the College of Physicians in 1664. The considerable part that he took in the rebuilding of London after the Great Fire of 1666 apparently roused his interest in selling fire insurance, and about 1680 he set up an office in London for that purpose.
Barbon’s writings on economics to some extent anticipated the conclusions of Adam Smith on the division of labour and the theory of currency as expounded by David Ricardo. His works include Apology for the Builder; or, A Discourse Showing the Cause and Effects of the Increase of Building (1685); A Discourse of Trade (1690); and A Discourse Concerning Coining the New Money Lighter (1696).

url_citation.content:
In September 1666, the Great Fire of London burned for four days and took roughly thirteen thousand houses with it. When the smoke cleared, the city faced a question that was less about grief than about mortar: who would rebuild, how fast, and on whose terms. Into that opening stepped a man named Nicholas Barbon — trained as a physician, temperamentally a speculator — who bought up ruined lots, threw up terraces, and became one of the first large-scale property developers London had ever seen. He also picked up a pen. In 1685 he published a short pamphlet with a defensive-sounding title, An Apology for the Builder, and set out to argue that the men everyone loved to blame were, in fact, quietly making the country richer.
The complaint Barbon was answering is one we would recognize.
